chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Yahya al-Azraq, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the man who is killed and leaves a debt, and has no wealth, so his guardians take the blood money (diyah). Is it upon them to pay off his debt? He (peace be upon him) said: 'Yes.' I said: 'And if he had not left anything [else]?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Yes. They took his blood money, therefore it is upon them to pay off his debt.'

key_terms.أَوْلِيَاؤُهُ: Heirs or guardians, those entitled to receive the blood money.
key_terms.الدَّيْن: Debt, financial obligation owed by the deceased.
key_terms.الدِّيَة: Blood money or wergild, compensation paid to the heirs of a victim of homicide or injury.
key_terms.يَقْضُوا: To pay off or settle (a debt).

ai.seo_question: Who is responsible for paying the debts of a person killed in action or murdered who left no other wealth?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the obligation to settle debts from blood money (diyah) rests upon the heirs who receive it, establishing a clear hierarchy of financial claims in Shia jurisprudence. This ruling underscores the principle that the deceased's creditors hold priority over heirs' personal gain, ensuring that the 'right of the servant' (haqq al-'abd) is fulfilled before the 'right of God' or personal inheritance is distributed. The hadith highlights the practical application of debt settlement in cases of violent death, where the estate may consist solely of the compensation paid for the life lost.
